lessons.title: Building a Portfolio That Survives the Next Crash

body.text: You cannot predict the next crash. You can build a portfolio, and a plan, that lets you live through it without ever being forced to sell.

children.text: This course has taken you from margin buyers on Wall Street in 1929 to first-time investors on Zerodha in March 2020. The investors who were destroyed by those crashes were rarely the ones who failed to predict them. They were the ones who were forced to sell: by margin calls, by loans, by needing the money too soon, or by their own panic. This final lesson turns everything you have learned into seven practical layers of protection. None of them requires you to know when the next crash is coming.
Crash-Proof Is a Myth. Crash-Survivable Is the Goal.

No portfolio that owns shares can avoid falling when markets crash. A portfolio is crash-survivable if, when the next 40% fall arrives, you are not forced to sell, your important goals remain on track, and you have the cash and the calm to stick to your plan or even take advantage of lower prices.

body.caption: Seven Layers of a Crash-Survivable Portfolio

cells: Being forced to sell investments to pay for a job loss, illness or emergency
Needing money that is invested in shares just as they crash
IPO investors in 2008 who needed their money back
One stock or theme wiping out a large share of your wealth
Unitech, Zee Telefilms and the K-10 stocks
Margin calls and forced selling at the bottom
Stopping investments or holding the wrong mix after a crash
Investors who sold in October 2008 or March 2020

children.text: Layer 1: The Emergency Fund and Insurance

markDefs.definition: Money kept in safe, easily accessible places such as a savings account, fixed deposit or liquid fund, to cover several months of essential expenses in case of job loss, illness or other emergencies.

children.text: The first layer has nothing to do with markets. An
emergency fund

of several months of essential expenses, held in safe and accessible places, means a job loss during a crash does not force you to sell shares at their lowest prices. Adequate health insurance and, if others depend on your income, term life insurance do the same for medical emergencies and worse. In March 2020, the investors who could leave their portfolios alone were very often the ones who never needed to touch them.
Layer 2: Match Your Money to Your Time

The most common way crashes ruin people is not the fall itself, but needing the money before prices recover. The Nifty regained its 2020 peak in under a year, but the Sensex took nearly three years after 2008, and the Nasdaq took 15 years after 2000. Money you will need soon does not belong in assets that can take years to recover.

body.caption: A Common Educational Framework: Matching Investments to Time Horizon

cells: Savings account, fixed deposits, liquid funds
Safety and access matter far more than returns
Fixed deposits, short duration debt funds
Too short to reliably ride out an equity crash
A mix of debt and equity
Some growth, but still vulnerable to a long bear market
Equity-oriented, alongside some debt and gold for balance
Enough time for markets to recover from most crashes

body.title: The Same 40% Crash, Two Different Goals

columns.label: Money Needed in 18 Months
points: A down payment for a flat, invested fully in equity funds
The crash cuts ₹10 lakh to ₹6 lakh
No time to wait for a recovery
Either the goal is delayed or losses are locked in by selling
The problem was the choice of asset, not the crash

columns.label: Money Needed in 15 Years
points: A child's higher education fund, invested in equity funds
The same crash cuts ₹10 lakh to ₹6 lakh on paper
Many years remain for the market to recover
Ongoing SIPs buy more units at lower prices
The crash is painful but survivable

children.text: Layer 3: Diversify Across Assets That Behave Differently

markDefs.definition: How a portfolio is divided between broad asset classes such as equity, debt and gold. It is the biggest single driver of how much a portfolio falls in a crash.

children.text: Owning fifty stocks is not real diversification if they all crash together.
Asset allocation
across assets that tend to behave differently matters more. In both of India's biggest recent crashes, gold moved in the opposite direction to shares.

stats.label: Gold in Rupees, 2008
stats.context: Based on average annual prices per 10 grams

body.title: An Illustrative Balanced Allocation (not a recommendation)
Your Turn: How Much Does Diversification Cushion a Crash?
body.prompt: A ₹10 lakh portfolio holds ₹6 lakh in equity, ₹3 lakh in debt and ₹1 lakh in gold. In a crash, equity falls 40%, debt rises 5% and gold rises 20%. By what percentage does the whole portfolio fall? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Equity: ₹6 lakh × 0.60 = ₹3.6 lakh. Debt: ₹3 lakh × 1.05 = ₹3.15 lakh. Gold: ₹1 lakh × 1.20 = ₹1.2 lakh. Total = ₹7.95 lakh, a fall of about 20.5%. An all-equity portfolio would have fallen 40%. The balanced portfolio fell about half as much, which makes it far easier to hold on without panicking. These returns are illustrative; in real crashes, debt and gold do not always rise.

body.text: Diversification reduces damage; it does not guarantee that anything will rise in a crash. In a scramble for cash, almost every asset can fall at the same time, at least briefly, and lower rated debt can suffer badly, as Franklin Templeton's investors discovered in 2020. Diversify across asset quality too, not just asset type.

children.text: Layer 4: Limit Any Single Bet

markDefs.definition: Deciding how much of a portfolio to put into any single stock, fund or theme, so that no single failure can do irreparable damage.

children.text: The K-10 stocks, Unitech and many dot-com favourites fell 90% or more and never came back to their peaks. A diversified index can recover from a crash; an individual company may not.
Position sizing
decides whether one such collapse is a setback or a disaster.

body.caption: What a 90% Collapse in One Stock Does to a ₹10 Lakh Portfolio
headers: Share of Portfolio in That Stock

children.text: Layer 5: Keep Leverage Out of Long-Term Money

You have seen this thread in every chapter. Borrowed money, whether through margin, MTF, F&O or loans against shares, turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss, because it can force you to sell at the bottom. As Lesson 5.1 showed, at 5x leverage a 20% fall wipes you out, and the Sensex fell 13% on a single day in March 2020. For money meant to grow over many years, the simplest rule is also the most powerful: do not borrow to invest it.
Layer 6: Let SIPs and Rebalancing Work Through the Crash

markDefs.definition: Investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals, usually monthly. Because the amount is fixed, it automatically buys more units when prices are low and fewer when prices are high.

children.text: A
Systematic Investment Plan (SIP)

turns a crash from a threat into an opportunity, but only if it keeps running. Look at a simple illustrative example: an index falls from 100 to 60 over a year, then climbs back to exactly 100 over the next year.

body.title: An Illustrative Crash and Recovery: Index Level Over 24 Months

body.label: SIP Through the Crash (illustrative)
body.context: A ₹10,000 monthly SIP for 24 months, through a fall from 100 to 60 and back to 100, ends up about 27.7% ahead, even though the index finished exactly where it started. The crash let the SIP buy units at an average price of about 78.3. Stopping the SIP at the bottom would have given up that advantage.

markDefs.definition: Periodically bringing a portfolio back to its target asset allocation, which means selling some of what has risen and buying more of what has fallen.

children.text: The second tool is
rebalancing

. A crash automatically shrinks your equity share. Take a ₹10 lakh portfolio at 60% equity and 40% debt. If equity falls 40% and debt is unchanged, the portfolio is worth ₹7,60,000 and equity is now only about 47% of it. Rebalancing means moving money from debt back into equity to restore 60%, buying shares when they are cheap. Here is what happens if equity then recovers to its original level.

body.caption: Rebalancing After a Crash (illustrative, debt returns and costs ignored)

body.text: Rebalancing forces you to do the hardest thing in investing: buy what everyone is afraid of. It works best as a rule decided in advance, for example rebalancing once a year or whenever an asset moves more than 5 to 10 percentage points from its target. In practice, selling to rebalance can trigger taxes and exit loads, so directing new SIP money towards the asset that has fallen is often a simpler way to rebalance.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Bringing a portfolio back to its target mix, by selling some of what has risen and buying more of what has fallen, is called ___.
body.explanation: Rebalancing keeps your risk at the level you chose, and in a crash it quietly turns your plan into a buyer of cheap assets, without requiring you to predict the bottom.

children.text: Layer 7: Write Your Crash Plan Before the Crash

markDefs.definition: A short written document setting out your goals, time horizons, target asset allocation, rebalancing rules and what you will and will not do during market falls.

children.text: Every crash in this course was full of people who knew what they should do and did the opposite on the worst day. The answer is to decide in calm times and write it down. Professionals call this an
investment policy statement
. Yours can fit on one page.

body.title: Write Your One-Page Crash Plan
steps: List your main financial goals, the amount needed for each and the year you will need it
Confirm your emergency fund size and where it is kept, separate from investments
Write down your target allocation between equity, debt and gold for your long-term money
Set a maximum share of your portfolio for any single stock and any single theme
State in writing that you will not use margin, MTF or F&O with long-term money
Choose your rebalancing rule: a fixed date each year, or a threshold such as a 5 or 10 percentage point drift
Write the sentence: "If the market falls 30% or more, I will..." and complete it with specific actions, such as continuing SIPs and rebalancing
Sign and date it, and read it again before making any decision in the next crash

body.title: Three Investors, One Crash
body.scenario: The Nifty falls 35% over three months. Arvind, 31, has ₹8 lakh in shares and trades Nifty options using borrowed money, with no emergency fund. Meena, 45, has ₹25 lakh entirely in small cap funds, which she plans to use for her daughter's college fees in 18 months. Farhan, 38, has ₹20 lakh split 60% equity funds, 30% debt funds and 10% gold, six months of expenses in a fixed deposit, running SIPs, and a written plan to rebalance if equity drifts more than 10 percentage points from target.
body.prompt: For each investor, explain what the crash is likely to do to them and which of the seven layers they are missing.
body.modelAnswer: Arvind is the most vulnerable. He is missing layer 1, the emergency fund, and layer 5, keeping leverage out. Leveraged options positions can be wiped out in days, and borrowed money must be repaid regardless of what markets do, so he may be forced to sell his ₹8 lakh of shares at the bottom to cover losses or debts. Meena is missing layer 2, matching money to time, and layer 4, since her entire portfolio sits in one risky category. Small cap funds can fall more than the Nifty, and with fees due in 18 months she may not have time for a recovery, so she faces either locking in a large loss or failing to meet a key goal. Farhan has most layers in place. His diversified portfolio falls far less than the market because debt and gold cushion the equity decline; his emergency fund means he will not need to sell; his SIPs buy more units at lower prices; and his written rebalancing rule will trigger as equity drops, moving money into shares while they are cheap. His portfolio still falls, and the crash is still uncomfortable, but he is never forced to act against his own interests. The difference between the three is not intelligence or market forecasting. It is preparation done before the crash.

body.title: The Biggest Danger
body.question: Which situation is most likely to turn a temporary market crash into a permanent loss?
options: Holding a diversified equity mutual fund through a 30% fall
Continuing a monthly SIP while the market falls
Having borrowed money invested in shares when a margin call arrives near the bottom
Holding 10% of a portfolio in gold
body.explanation: A fall only becomes permanent when you sell at low prices. Margin calls force exactly that, at exactly the wrong moment. A diversified fund, a continuing SIP and a gold allocation all leave you in control of when, or whether, to sell.

children.text: This lesson gives you a framework, not a personal financial plan. Your right allocation depends on your income, dependants, goals, existing assets, tax situation and temperament.
For personalised advice:
consider a SEBI-registered investment adviser, who is required to act in your interest. You can check any adviser's registration on SEBI's website before paying them.
Be sceptical of guarantees:
anyone promising crash-proof returns, guaranteed income from shares or secret signals of the next crash is selling something you should not buy.
Keep learning:
revisit the warning sign scorecard from Lesson 5.1 twice a year, and reread your crash plan whenever markets feel either euphoric or terrifying.

body.label: SEBI: Check an Adviser's Registration
body.description: Before taking advice from anyone on what to buy or sell, search SEBI's list of registered intermediaries to confirm they are a registered investment adviser or research analyst.

cards.definition: A portfolio that will still fall in a crash, but where you are never forced to sell and your key goals stay on track.
Several months of essential expenses held in safe, accessible places, so a crisis never forces you to sell investments.
How a portfolio is split between equity, debt, gold and other assets. It drives how much a portfolio falls in a crash.
Limiting how much goes into any one stock or theme, so no single failure can do irreparable damage.
A Systematic Investment Plan: a fixed regular investment that buys more units when prices fall.
Restoring a portfolio to its target mix by trimming what has risen and adding to what has fallen.
A written plan setting out your goals, allocation, rebalancing rules and what you will do in a crash.

points: You cannot predict crashes, but you can avoid being forced to sell, which is what turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss
Build an emergency fund and adequate insurance first, and never keep money you need within a few years in assets that can take years to recover
Diversify across assets that behave differently: in 2008 and 2020, gold rose about 31% and 28% in rupees while Indian shares crashed
Limit any single stock or theme, because indices recover from crashes but individual companies may not
Keep leverage away from long-term money, keep SIPs running, and rebalance by rule: in the illustrative example, a SIP through a crash ended about 28% ahead even though the index ended flat
Write a one-page crash plan in calm times, so that on the next day like 23 March 2020 you follow your plan rather than your fear

body.text: Every crash in this course was eventually followed by a recovery in the broad market, though some took decades. The investors who benefited were not the ones who saw it coming. They were the ones who were still invested when it arrived.

This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment, financial or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy or sell any security or product. The allocations, returns and examples shown are illustrative and simplified, and ignore costs and taxes. Past recoveries do not guarantee future ones; individual securities may never recover. Consider consulting a SEBI-registered investment adviser for advice specific to your situation.
